title: The Third Rule: Every Push Has a Pull

t: You push a wall. The wall does not move. But you go backward. What pushed you?
Push a wall. You go backward. Something pushed you — what?
You push a wall. The wall pushes you back with the same force. Why don't you both move equally?
Newton's third law: forces come in equal and opposite pairs. Why does the wall stay put while you recoil?
sub: Nothing visible touched you. But something did — the wall pushed back.
The wall pushed you. Every push has an equal push back. That is the third rule.
The wall exerted an equal and opposite force on you. Newton's third law: forces occur in pairs.
The contact force from the wall on you is equal and opposite to your force on the wall. F_AB = -F_BA.

question: You are on roller skates. You push a heavy truck. What happens to YOU?
On roller skates, you push a stationary truck. What happens to you?
You push a massive truck while on frictionless skates. Describe your subsequent motion.
A person on frictionless skates exerts a force F on a truck of mass M >> m_person. What happens to the person?
options: You roll backward — the truck pushed you back, even though it barely moved
Nothing happens to you — the truck is too heavy
You go forward — the push carried you along
stages.outcome: You roll backward — the truck pushed you back, even though it barely moved
note: Most people forget about themselves. Think about what the truck did to you.
Predict — and remember: the push goes both ways.
Form a hypothesis. Apply F_AB = -F_BA to both bodies.
Predict. The truck exerts -F on you; by F = ma, your acceleration is F/m, much larger than the truck's F/M.

stages.label: Who is pushing who?
captions: You push the trolley. The trolley goes forward.
The trolley pushes you back. You go backward (if you are on skates).
Both pushes are the same size. The trolley moves more because it is lighter — not because the push is bigger.
Every push in the world comes with an equal push back. They are a pair — you never get one without the other.
t: Move the slider. See the same push from both sides.
Drag the slider. The same push, seen from both ends.
after: Two pushes, same size, opposite directions. That is every push in the universe.
F_AB = -F_BA. Action and reaction are equal, opposite, and simultaneous.

stages.label: Action-reaction pairs
captions: You push the trolley forward. The trolley pushes you backward. F_you→trolley = -F_trolley→you.
The Earth pulls you down (gravity). You pull the Earth up. Same force, opposite directions — the Earth just barely moves because it is so massive.
A rocket pushes gas backward. The gas pushes the rocket forward. No ground needed — that is why rockets work in space.
You walk by pushing the ground backward. The ground pushes you forward. Walking is a series of action-reaction pairs with the Earth.
t: Work out the pair before the caption arrives.
Predict the reaction force before reading each caption. Identify the pair, not just one side.
after: Every one of these is the same rule: forces come in pairs, equal and opposite. The third law.
Newton's third law: F_AB = -F_BA for all forces, gravitational, electromagnetic, and contact. There are no unpaired forces.

t: Every push has an equal push back. That is the third rule.
Every push has an equal push in the opposite direction. That is Newton's third law.
Newton's third law: for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. The two forces act on different bodies.
Newton's third law: F_AB = -F_BA. The action-reaction pair acts on different bodies, so they do not cancel. They are simultaneous, equal, and opposite.
sub: The pushes are the same size. The movement is different because the masses are different.
Why don't the forces cancel? Because they push on different things — one on you, one on the wall.
The pair never cancels because they act on different bodies. The Earth feels your weight; you feel the Earth's pull. Both are real.
Action-reaction pairs act on different systems. Choosing the system determines which member is relevant to the analysis.

t: Rockets work in space because they push gas backward, and the gas pushes them forward. No air needed.
A rocket pushes gas out the back. The gas pushes the rocket forward. This works in space — no air needed.
Rocket propulsion is pure third law: expel mass backward, accelerate forward. The vacuum of space is not an obstacle; it is the point.
The Tsiolkovsky equation and all reaction propulsion derive from conservation of momentum, which is equivalent to Newton's third law integrated over time.

q: You push a wall. The wall pushes you. Which push is bigger?
You exert 50 N on a wall. What force does the wall exert on you?
You push a wall with force F. What is the reaction force on you?
You exert F on a wall. What is the magnitude and direction of the wall's force on you?
options: The same size — every push has an equal push back
The wall pushes harder — it is solid
The wall does not push — it just stops you
why: The wall pushes you with exactly the same force you pushed it. That is the third law — every push has an equal push back, on the other thing.
The wall pushes back with 50 N. Newton's third law: the forces are equal and opposite. The wall does not move because it is attached to the Earth; you move because you are not.
F_wall→you = -F_you→wall = -50 N (opposite direction, same magnitude). The wall's rigidity transmits the force to the Earth, which absorbs the recoil invisibly.
F_AB = -F_BA. The wall exerts -F on you. The Earth-wall system acquires momentum -p; you acquire +p. The Earth's enormous mass makes its motion undetectable.

q: Why do the action and reaction forces not cancel each other out?
If action = -reaction, why don't they cancel?
Newton's third law says F_AB = -F_BA. Why doesn't the net force on the system vanish?
If action and reaction are equal and opposite, why is there any acceleration at all?
options: They push on different things, so they do not cancel
They do cancel — that is why nothing moves
why: You push the wall. The wall pushes you. One push is on the wall, one is on you. They do not cancel because they are on different things.
The action force is on the wall. The reaction force is on you. They act on different objects, so neither object experiences both — no cancellation.
Action and reaction act on different bodies. The wall feels only your push; you feel only the wall's push. Neither body experiences a net zero from the pair.

F_AB acts on B; F_BA acts on A. They are equal and opposite but act on different systems. The net force on the combined system A+B is zero (momentum conserved), but each body accelerates according to the force on it alone.
